# Why Does My ALT Fuse Keep Blowing?

When you ground out the alternator lead battery wire and immediately find yourself replacing a 120-amp fuse, the issue isn't simply a bad component; it's an electrical fault that exceeds the circuit's protection threshold. In your specific scenario, where the fuse blows upon attempting to restart after grounding the alternator, the system is likely experiencing a direct short or an excessive load draw that triggers the breaker before the engine can even turn over.

The alternator (ALT) circuit is designed to handle significant current while charging the battery and powering accessories. A 120-amp fuse is a standard safety device for this high-current path, but it is not indestructible. If you have rewired the battery lead on the alternator and are seeing consistent failures despite clean contacts, the problem usually lies in how that ground connection interfaces with the vehicle's chassis or existing wiring harness.

When you physically disconnect the main power lead from the alternator to ground it, you alter the current path. Normally, current flows from the alternator through the output cable into the fuse box, then to the battery and grounds. By grounding the wire directly at the alternator terminal (or creating a bypass), you may have inadvertently created a low-resistance path that allows massive current to flow instantly when the ignition is turned on or when the starter engages. This surge trips the 120-amp fuse almost immediately, often before any diagnostic tool can register a voltage drop.

One common pitfall in rewiring alternator grounds is ensuring the new ground strap has lower resistance than the original path. If the new connection points to a corroded chassis bolt or a thin wire instead of a massive ground bus bar, the resulting heat and voltage drop can cause arcing. This arcing effectively shorts the circuit, blowing the fuse. Even if your contacts appear clean visually, oxidation beneath the surface or paint acting as an insulator can create intermittent high resistance that manifests as a short when thermal expansion occurs during operation.

Consider the state of the battery itself. If the vehicle was dead before you grounded the alternator lead and you attempted to crank without ensuring the battery had sufficient charge, the starter motor might be drawing more than 100 amps just to turn over. While this is normal for a starter circuit, if the alternator's internal diode bridge has failed (a common issue known as "internal shorts"), it can feed current back into the battery or ground paths in reverse when the engine stops spinning. This feedback loop can trip protective fuses designed to isolate the charging system.

To diagnose this without blowing another fuse, avoid simply reconnecting power and trying again. Use a multimeter to check for continuity between the alternator's main output terminal and the vehicle chassis with the ignition off. You should see near-zero resistance only if there is a confirmed short; however, if you are getting continuity where there shouldn't be any path, your rewiring has bypassed the intended isolation.

Additionally, verify that the ground point on the chassis is not connected to other sensitive circuits, such as fuel pumps or ECU grounds. Connecting high-current alternator grounds to low-current data lines can cause voltage spikes that blow fuses protecting those secondary systems. Ensure the new wiring uses appropriate gauge wire—typically 4 AWG or thicker for main alternator outputs—to handle the amperage without melting insulation, which could also appear as a short.

If you have ruled out bad connections and incorrect grounding points, the alternator itself may be internally damaged. A failing voltage regulator can cause the alternator to output excessive voltage, forcing the 120-amp fuse to open as a last resort against overheating components in the wiring harness. In such cases, replacing the alternator or its internal regulator is often more effective than continuing to troubleshoot external wiring loops.
